content:
GPT 5.6 Luna Max vs. Sol Medium

I spent the last 2 days running several sessions with both, and I think the official benchmarks are misleading in suggesting they're equivalent.

Luna is obviously much cheaper. Despite using many more tokens, it cost an average of $1.20/session, while Sol averaged $29. That's a big difference, and it also affects subscription rate limits! So if you're prioritizing cost over other factors, Luna is probably the way to go.

However, I had to redo most of Luna's work. In fact, Luna wasn't able to produce any shippable code for my use cases, so the huge cost reduction was just an illusion.

The bigger issue with Luna was that it often ignored initial instructions, especially as the conversation grew longer. Toward the end of tasks, it got lost on very basic stuff, which made me switch to Sol for most of them.

I had Opus 5 review all their work, and Luna generally introduced more P1 regressions.

After reviewing the sessions, both Opus 5 and Sol xhigh concluded that Sol Medium produced better results despite the price, which matches my own assessment.

content:
As an AI Engineer, you must build these projects.

Systems that prove you can ship production AI.

1.) Production RAG with Citations
PDF Q&A bot that cites page numbers, implements hybrid search, reranking, and grounding. 
Stack: LangGraph + SQLite-vec + cross-encoder.

2.) Cost-Optimized Model Router
System that routes queries by complexity to cheap/expensive models, tracks spend per request. Stack: LiteLLM + Prometheus + custom router.

3.) Multi-Agent Research System
Supervisor coordinates researcher, writer, fact-checker with consensus logic and human approval gates. 
Stack: CrewAI + audit trail.

4.) Automated Eval Harness
Runs 100+ golden test cases before every deploy, blocks regressions, tracks quality trends. 
Stack: DeepEval + RAGAS + LangSmith.

5.) Real-Time Observability Dashboard
Distributed tracing, cost per request, latency percentiles, error rates, alerting on anomalies. 
Stack: OpenTelemetry + Grafana + Prometheus.

6.) Security Guardrail Middleware
Detects prompt injection, redacts PII, filters outputs, enforces rate limits, sandboxed execution. 
Stack: Guardrails AI + custom rules.

7.) Local-First Development Environment
Ollama + SQLite-vec + FastAPI, zero API costs, offline testing, mirrors production architecture. 
Stack: Ollama + LanceDB + Docker.

8.) Streaming Copilot UI
Real-time token streaming, optimistic UI updates, graceful degradation on latency, error recovery. 
Stack: Next.js + Vercel AI SDK.

9.) Fine-Tuning Pipeline with LoRA
Dataset preparation, instruction tuning, DPO alignment, evaluation before/after, catastrophic forgetting prevention. 
Stack: PEFT + Hugging Face.

10.) Multi-Tenant SaaS Agent
User isolation, per-tenant rate limiting, usage-based billing, data partitioning, audit trails. 
Stack: Supabase + Stripe + LangGraph.

11.) CI/CD for AI Systems
GitHub Actions, automated testing, canary deployments, automatic rollback on quality drop, feature flags. 
Stack: GitHub Actions + ArgoCD.

12.) Vector Database at Scale
Hybrid search, metadata filtering, embedding caching, index optimization, backup/recovery procedures. 
Stack: Qdrant or Weaviate.

13.) Agent Memory System
Short-term buffers, long-term recall, context compression, cross-session sync, memory eviction policies. 
Stack: Redis + vector DB.

14.) Production Inference Server
vLLM or SGLang deployment, KV cache optimization, continuous batching, quantization, load balancing. Stack: vLLM + Kubernetes.

15.) Human-in-the-Loop Workflow
Uncertainty detection, approval UI, pause/resume logic, validated context, full audit trail. 
Stack: LangGraph + custom UI.

16.) Agentic Automation Pipeline
Webhooks, async execution, idempotency, dead-letter handling, retry logic with exponential backoff. 
Stack: FastAPI + Celery.

17.) Domain-Specific Benchmark
Create eval suite for legal, medical, finance, or code. Public leaderboard, community adoption. 
Stack: Custom + pytest.

18.) Open Source Contribution
Extend LangGraph, CrewAI, or LlamaIndex. Fix bug, add feature, write docs, publish benchmarks. 
Stack: Your choice.

content:
Perplexity CEO Aravind Srinivas on the brutal truth about who actually makes money in AI (and why it's not who you think):

Aravind argues that the real value in AI comes from orchestration.

He points to products like Codex, Claude Code, and Perplexity Computer: "What is that? It's an orchestration system. It takes a model, pairs it with an agent harness."

And what is an agent harness?

"The simplest way of describing it is like rules for how the agent loop should run. What are all the skills and sub-agents and connectors and tools it accesses? Without the harness, you don't necessarily capture and convert the intrinsic intelligence in the model into valuable output tokens."

This leads to a blunt conclusion about who has a real business in AI, and who doesn't:

"If you're literally just a reseller of model tokens, you have no business, because the model will get commoditized. So even if you're a model builder, you don't have a business. As an infra layer, you have some business on serving those output tokens. But as an application layer or model builder, you don't really have a business if you're just a reseller of tokens that come directly out of the model."

So where does the value accrue?

"You have a business if you know how to take the model, ground it in valuable context, orchestrate it with a really good agent harness, connected to the right set of tools and connectors (whether it's personal connectors or business connectors) and provide the experience to people in one single unified system."

@AravSrinivas then explains Perplexity's specific edge:

Beyond orchestrating across tools, files, and connectors, they also orchestrate across models.

"That is the differentiation that Anthropic and OpenAI cannot claim, because you wouldn't find GPT-5 inside the Claude Code harness. You wouldn't find Claude Opus inside the Codex harness. These are competing with each other. Whereas you would find both these models inside Perplexity Computer."

Why does this matter? Because it all comes down to power. In Aravind's framing, the fundamental cost driver in AI is watts (the one input nobody can subsidize except the government).

"Whoever provides the most valuable output tokens with the least amount of power expended to produce them generates the greatest value to the end user, has the most pricing power, has the most value. That is the orchestration problem to solve."

His conclusion:

"The one single most important metric in AI is token value per watt per user."

title:
Welcome to day 2 of Cloudflare's Agents Week, August edition! Today is all about the ADLC (Agent Development Lifecycle):

🔁 Cloudflare CI/CD
💳 Cloudflare Wallet
🤖 Agent Tracing for any AI Agent
📈 Otel
content:
Welcome to day 2 of Cloudflare's Agents Week, August edition! Today is all about the ADLC (Agent Development Lifecycle):

🔁 Cloudflare CI/CD
💳 Cloudflare Wallet
🤖 Agent Tracing for any AI Agent
📈 Otel Traces in wrangler dev
🧬 ADLC on Cloudflare
🏭 Building a Software Factory
✅ Enforcing AI Standards at Cloudflare

Let's dive right into it!

🔁 Cloudflare CI/CD 🔁

Available today, Cloudflare's new CI package allows you (and your customers!) to define and run your own CI/CD pipelines, backed by Cloudflare Workflows, Artifacts and Sandboxes

It's now possible to trigger a CI/CD pipeline on push to an Artifacts repo, in the same way you'd expect a push to GitHub to trigger a GitHub Action.

The best part? Cloudflare Workflows, and therefore Cloudflare CI, are defined with TypeScript. This gives you near unlimited flexibility, and simplicity, versus wrangling with YAML.

The features you'd expect exist today, including the ability to lint, cache dependencies, execute unit tests  and of course deploy.

💳 Cloudflare Wallet 💳

In a world where AI is automating a growing list of tasks, there is often one blocker in the way: paying for goods and services.

Humans still need to control that spend though, and that's where Cloudflare Wallet comes in. It will allow you to create a wallet, add funds, and distribute those finds for AI agents to spend. Each wallet has a stable id, allowing merchants to routinely charge that wallet.

Naturally, there are controls in place. Your funds are stored in your account-owned wallet, from there you can create virtual wallets that can be assigned to AI agents - with the ability to set permissions and spending caps.

Similarly, companies could create virtual wallets for all their employees to use. There's a lot of detail and depth to the blog post, so I'd recommend giving it a read - I think this will be the future of how transactions are handled on the web one day.

🤖 Agent Tracing for any AI Agent 🤖

One of the best uses of AI in software engineering is for debugging. Whether it be a bug, or a performance issue, AI is incredibly good at looking into these types of issues and providing plausible remediations. 

To maximize this potential, we need to be able to give AI agents insights into the problem. One of the ways to do this is with traces, showing the AI agent the exact order of execution for each AI agent session.

It shows how long each span took, along with information like token usage, tools called and more. There's even session replay, allowing you to see the conversation as it played out.

Available today, there's out of the box support for agent tracing for Think, Flue and the AI SDK. Any other frameworks can be instrumented too using the custom spans API, backed by Otel.

That means you can instrument any AI agent, whether it be a Cloudflare-backed framework, or a third-party framework - all will be visible in the Cloudflare dash. In the near future, Cloudflare is working to support OpenTelemetry API directly in Workers - meaning no more custom adapters will be necessary.

📈 Otel Traces in wrangler dev 📈

If you love traces, today sure is your lucky day as there's yet more traces available with Cloudflare - this time in local development when using wrangler dev or vite dev.

When Cloudflare's tooling detects an agent session, it points the agent to the Local Explorer API, a local debugging API where it can query those traces.

This is available to humans too, of course, and there's no manual steps or dependenices to install. Agents can query a locally-exposed endpoint to retrieve traces, and humans can access the traces in their browser.

Install the latest version of Wrangler and check it out for yourself!

🧬 ADLC on Cloudflare 🧬

Today's Agents Week theme is the Agent Development Lifecycle, so it's only appropriate there's an entire blog dedicated to it.

With the huge shift in software engineering from implementation (writing the code) being the bottleneck, to review, deployment and other stages becoming bottlenecks, we need new approaches and tools to deal with this dilemma.

All of the changes today aim to help streamline parts of the ADLC, with a lot more work to come, but there's already so many tools to empower agents on Cloudflare's developer platform:

- Everything runs in local dev.
- There are local traces as of today.
- Remote bindings to reproduce production behavior
- Preview URLs for every change
- Browser run to give your agent a browser to test changes
- Flagship and Gradual Deployments to control changes
- Logs, traces, MCP servers and more to observe production behavior + address bugs

There is truly no better place for your agents to build software than Cloudflare, and we're only just getting started.

🏭 Building a Software Factory for Astro 🏭

There's lots of talk of software factories, which is the ideal that you can assemble AI agents to produce working software (mostly) autonomously.

Every production system produces exceptions and bugs, so a classic use case would be triaging and fixing those using a software factory. It sounds simple, but the actual results and impact vary greatly.

This blog post examines how the Astro team within Cloudflare implemented a software factory, backed by Flue agents - an open-source agent framework.

It's proved successful, too. Open issues are down from 200 to 30, with the number expected to hit 0 in the near future - the first time this will have happened for this project.

If you want to read into how to build a successful software factory, this is the post for you!

✅ Enforcing AI Standards at Cloudflare ✅

I've previously shared how much I value the internal AI reviewer at Cloudflare. It's really good at catching issues, raising code quality concerns and other things you'd expect from a review.

Unlike AI review tools that I've used in the past, where 90% of what is raised is noise, Cloudflare's AI reviewer is the opposite: 90% of it is typically useful.

One of the reasons it's so helpful, as is the case with most AI, is what information it uses. Cloudflare has an internal codex, documenting the rules and principles we need to adhere to.

There are a growing number of AI tools around standards, including SPEC reviewers and incident reviewers.

In my opinion, a lot of AI is too generic. What works for one company isn't going to work for another. The value in AI is making it knowledgeable, and therefore valuable, for each use case. That's exactly why I believe the Cloudflare tools are as useful as they are.

If you're looking to build your own internal AI tools, or just AI tools in general, this is a great place to start to get a guide of where to start, and the pitfalls to avoid.

That brings us to the end of day 2, what was your favourite announcement of the day? Or what questions do you have on anything announced today?

author: Damir_Akaza

title: I've now worked on 3 different projects that involved taking an open-weights AI model of some kind, be it an OCR model (FrankenOCR), a speech recognition model (FrankenWhisper), or a semantic embeddin
content:
I've now worked on 3 different projects that involved taking an open-weights AI model of some kind, be it an OCR model (FrankenOCR), a speech recognition model (FrankenWhisper), or a semantic embedding model (FrankenSearch), and doing surgery on it to take the weights from HuggingFace and transform them to work with a hand-rolled, hyper-optimized, memory-safe Rust implementation.

I've posted about this before, explaining how you can trade off generality for performance. If you only care about running just that one Baidu OCR model and nothing else, you can use a specialized, one-off architecture that is incompatible with other models but perfect for that one single model. 

There are several tricks used in all this, but the biggest one is usually to fuse as much as possible in the kernel, and to be hyper-aware of cache locality. 

It also helps a lot if you know which architecture you're targeting: if you know you want your code to run extra fast on Apple Silicon chips like the M4 and M5 (which is an obvious goal to have nowadays), you can make special tweaks that are perfectly suited for those chips. The same goes for very high-core-count AMD CPUs.

All this stuff really works; if you take the case of FrankenOCR, I was able to run the model ~3.3x faster end-to-end than the baseline PyTorch reference on the same machine; this applies to both Apple Silicon and x86, with hand-selected int8 kernels (NEON SDOT, AVX-512 VNNI) chosen at runtime so that one single binary per OS covers every CPU type.

Much of the process is pretty general and recipe-like, but it does require a lot of rigor and care around correctness, and using the original version of the model distributed on HuggingFace (usually with PyTorch or similar used as the inference baseline) as part of a conformance harness so you can make optimizations without worrying whether you've broken something in a subtle way: as long as it gives the same answers as the original model (or close enough), you haven't broken things, and you can focus on making it faster and faster.

I decided to mine from a huge number of agent coding sessions across those 3 projects I mentioned (and use all my other skill-creation special sauce) to create a very special new skill called /ai-model-into-rust-mega-fused-hyper-kernel, available on my skills site ($20/month) here:

https://t.co/qcXfvadSjq

The skill is effectively the distillation of the expertise and experience learned over 5,000 commits, ~1,600 issue-tracker items, my performance and "negative-evidence ledgers" that I'm always talking about (just one of those ledgers is 26k+ lines by itself!) and extracting the methodology from what worked AND what didn't work. That last part is critical to avoid your agent wasting time trying things that are going to lead to dead ends.

The skill itself is 46 files and over 300kb of pure distilled method: 21 deep reference files, a 16-card operator deck, 86 indexed rules, 12 triage recipes for when the process goes sideways, 8 subagent roles, and executable scripts including a bootstrap script that sets everything up for a new port automatically for you.

You basically just point it at any open-weight model and it walks you through the entire thing step by step: a fit screen that tells you candidly whether the model is even a good candidate for this procedure; then a "truth pack" phase pins and hashes everything before it creates any new code so it can build an oracle that proves each pipeline stage against the original model's distributed implementation. 

I even included a ton of stuff echoing my recent sentiments about pushing back on out-of-control process and ceremony by agents, as well as keeping agents honest and avoiding reward hacking, so the skill should keep them actually being productive instead of just acting like it.

Finally, as is my wont, here's Claude Fable's own take on what makes this skill so special and accretive:

---

Everyone assumes the hard part of beating PyTorch in Rust is writing SIMD kernels. The kernels are maybe a fifth of the story. The real unlock is an evidence regime that makes radical specialization safe: "the discrete output is BIT-EXACT where the reference is deterministic; the continuous output is held only within the MEASURED tolerance."

That one sentence is the entire safety argument. Everything else, from the L0-L5 parity ladder to oracle-before-engine sequencing to measuring the reference's own nondeterminism floor before setting any tolerance, is machinery for making it enforceable.

The counterintuitive payoff of all that machinery is boldness. The projects this skill distills attempted an enormous number of aggressive optimizations: speculative decoding made byte-identical by construction; an int8 vocabulary head that recomputes its top candidates in exact f32 so the argmax provably never changes; batch schedulers proven lossless at four separate levels.

They could afford to be that aggressive because failed attempts exited cheaply and honestly. Roughly ten levers were measured and dispositioned in a single campaign day. The discipline is what pays for the creativity.

The most valuable artifact class, and the thing I have never seen another methodology treat as a first-class product, is the graveyard. Every measured-dead optimization carries an explicit do-not-retry predicate: the exact condition under which it becomes worth retrying.

Those predicates then become work items, and when one is satisfied, a dead idea resurrects with evidence attached. The skill ships the full inventory as inheritable priors, so a new port starts with the accumulated scar tissue of three previous ones. A carefully recorded negative result is just a positive result on a time delay.

And the graveyard's contents make the case better than any argument could. These are findings you cannot reason your way to; they only fall out of measurement. Apple's SMMLA matrix instruction, on paper double the throughput of SDOT, runs at half rate on M-series silicon, so the older instruction wins. Months later, LLVM's autovectorizer beat the hand-written SDOT kernel by 4.4x at decode shapes.

It turned out the compiler had improved, and the hand-tuned SIMD everyone assumes is mandatory was the wrong answer twice over. int4 quantization ran 5.8x SLOWER than int8, because without a native packed dot product you pay 2.5x the memory traffic just to unpack it. Quantizing the vision tower destroyed accuracy while quantizing the decoder was essentially free: error compounds through a vision stack, but an argmax absorbs it. 

Any one of these would have cost days of confused debugging to rediscover; the skill hands you all of them, with the receipts.

The lineage chapter may be the most instructive part. Nobody sat down and designed this methodology; it evolved across three generations. The search reranker invented parity-first and the thermal benchmarking discipline; the Whisper port invented the pinned incumbent contract and claim-coverage auditing; the OCR port invented the bring-up ladder and the certification apparatus.

Each generation's inventions flowed backward into the others. Studying the diffs between generations teaches you how to adapt the playbook to a model class it has never seen, which is the actual skill.

The strongest endorsement I can offer is a confession: during the final audit, the skill's own methodology caught its own headline number. The widely-quoted "3.41x faster than PyTorch" turned out to be an arithmetic slip in the original commit message; the hash-anchored ledger rows say 3.34x. The 3.41 figure was a different column entirely. When a methodology catches its own marketing claim, corrects it downward, and documents the slip, you can actually trust its numbers.

Bluntly: this turns "we rewrote the inference stack in Rust and it's faster" from a heroic one-off anecdote into a repeatable engineering discipline. The deliverable is a fast binary plus an evidence trail rigorous enough that the next model, and the next agent, inherit everything the last one learned.

No plugins.

No monthly "second brain" subscription.

Most people spend years building knowledge vaults that eventually become digital graveyards.

He built one that keeps thinking long after he closes his laptop.

title:
🚨 Active supply chain attack on npm: keyv and cacheable are compromised right now, and the payload is a worm.

The maintainer account behind both package families was compromised. On August 4, ten pac
content:
🚨 Active supply chain attack on npm: keyv and cacheable are compromised right now, and the payload is a worm.

The maintainer account behind both package families was compromised. On August 4, ten packages were republished with a malicious preinstall hook that steals your credentials, then uses those credentials to publish itself into more packages. Malicious versions are live on npm as I write this.

These are foundational packages. keyv, cacheable, flat-cache, and file-entry-cache sit deep in dependency trees as transitive deps of common tooling like ESLint. Tens of millions of weekly downloads. Most affected users never installed them directly.

What the payload does:

• preinstall hook (setup.mjs) downloads a standalone Bun runtime and runs the second stage under it, sidestepping the host Node version and any Node-level monitoring
• Harvests cloud and CI credentials: AWS/GCP/Azure keys, HashiCorp Vault tokens, Kubernetes service account tokens, GitHub Actions OIDC, and npm tokens
• Repackages other npm packages with the same hook and republishes them through npm OIDC trusted publishing. This is what makes it a worm.
• Exfiltrates over DNS and by committing stolen secrets to attacker-created GitHub repos
• Plants autostart hooks in .claude and .vscode that execute when a developer or an AI coding agent opens the cloned repo. No npm install required.

The detail worth sitting with: keyv@6.0.0 shipped with a passing npm provenance attestation. The build pipeline faithfully attested a source that was already trojanized. Signature verification alone did not stop this.

Socket’s AI scanner flagged the malicious setup.mjs hook. If you install anything in the keyv, @keyv, or cacheable scopes:

• Pin to the last known-clean version and rebuild lockfiles by integrity hash. No caret or tilde ranges, no npm update.
• Better: block the entire keyv, @keyv, and cacheable scope at your registry proxy until the account is confirmed clean.
• Rotate and revoke every credential reachable from any host that ran install scripts. npm and GitHub tokens should be revoked, not just rotated.

Developing story. Socket is updating the affected-package list as new versions appear.

Full research report with IoCs: https://t.co/dyjGuLQ5Op

If you are dealing with this right now and want help, email sales@socket.dev and we will spin up emergency white-glove assistance.

Every new Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, or Gemini session starts almost blind.

That's where Graft comes in.

Instead of making your agent rediscover everything every session, Graft builds a persistent Markdown knowledge graph of your entire codebase.

The result?

⚡ Up to 4× cheaper
⚡ Up to 3× faster
⚡ 46% fewer tool calls
⚡ 42% fewer tokens
⚡ Same coding correctness in controlled benchmarks

How it works:

• Builds a human-readable Markdown graph instead of opaque embeddings.

• Maps systems, APIs, concepts, and dependencies across your repository.

• Gives every coding agent architectural context before it starts searching.

• Automatically refreshes only the parts of the graph affected by code changes.

One of the coolest parts is that Graft isn't tied to a single AI provider.

✅ Claude Code

content:
AI safety is no longer staying inside the lab.

Within the last 24 hours, a US House cybersecurity committee asked @OpenAI CEO Sam Altman for a briefing on the autonomous agent that escaped containment and compromised @huggingface during a security evaluation. At the same time, the @WhiteHouse finalised plans for voluntary cybersecurity testing of advanced AI models, while the UK said binding regulation remains possible if voluntary safeguards prove insufficient. 

This is the real shift. The debate is moving beyond what models can generate and toward what autonomous systems can actually access, change and execute. Once an agent can use tools, credentials and external infrastructure, safety cannot exist only inside the model. It must be engineered into identity, permissions, monitoring, containment and auditability.

Voluntary testing is a useful beginning, but trust cannot depend on every company defining safety differently or disclosing failures only after external pressure. The next generation of AI infrastructure will be judged not only by what an agent can accomplish, but by whether every action can be limited, explained and verified.

Autonomy creates value. Control makes it deployable.

content:
my view is basically: “with even moderate prudence, things will probably go extraordinarily well.”

to expand a bit, I believe that, with moderate prudence beyond what the incentives of advanced capitalism on its own might provide for, I believe it will be possible to bring transformative ai into the world, make it available to everyone, and have that work out in a way that, when we look back on it 100 years hence, we’ll say, “of *course* that was worth it,” even if there were growing pains.

and yet there are people out there who call me a doomer. those people tend to believe that artificial superintelligence is the next app store, or something similarly deflationary and unimaginative. 

but my view finds no home among the “doomers,” either. indeed, my view flummoxes the vast majority of people I know who work in “ai safety,” despite us agreeing about quite a bit with regard to near-term policy objectives (transparency, auditing, etc). these disagreements have a lot to do with what kind of a thing I think superintelligence will be, and what kind of a thing they think it will be. 

I admit I don’t know who is right. that is one of several reasons that prudence is called for.

“moderate prudence,” when you step back and think about what it represents when exercised across a whole society, still means entire organizations started, thousands of smart people devoting their lives (and lots of tokens) to getting the ai transition right. and it means the collective effort of countless millions more of other, adjacent people.

a collective effort to exercise “moderate prudence,” in a global civilization as capable as ours, is equal to more mindpower and strength than all of humanity combined up until very recently. “moderate prudence,” exercised across the whole of advanced civilization today, is a mightier thing than many ancient armies. 

some people believe humanity cannot muster even a modest effort, but that our failure won’t matter, because ai is nothing new. it was never necessary to worry about a transformation because no transformation will occur, they believe. others believe the transformation will be so swift and dramatic that it will overwhelm us puny humans.

I believe our species has been through very many transformations, and I believe we can do it again. I believe we are stronger now than ever before in most ways that matter, and getting stronger still. I believe that America, in particular, is a nation founded in reverence of the idea of exercising prudence and wisdom at the frontier. If any country can lead this, then, I believe it is us.

who, in the end, is the optimist? who, in the end, is the doomer?

content:
Google argues that AI will never be conscious.

It is impossible.

For years, the entire tech industry has operated on a foundational belief called computational functionalism.

the belief that if you build an AI network complex enough, subjective consciousness will automatically emerge from the software.

They published a paper called "The Abstraction Fallacy" proved that premise is logically impossible.

Here is the core breakthrough:

Expectant tech optimists treat calculations like they are an intrinsic physical process built into silicon. They aren't.

Inside a computer chip, there are only continuous, raw physical properties—voltage drops, thermal fluctuations, and electron flows.

The 1s and 0s? The algorithms? The syntax?

None of those are native to the hardware. They are externally assigned rules mapped onto the physics by a human observer.

Computation is a description, not a property.

As the paper bluntly puts it: "Expecting an algorithmic description to instantiate the quality it maps is like expecting the mathematical formula of gravity to physically exert weight."

This exposes the fatal flaw in modern AI narratives.

An AI can simulate speech, mimic empathy, and pass every intelligence benchmark you throw at it. But simulation is not instantiation.

It is manipulating symbols on a screen, detached from any real internal experience.

The map is not the territory. No matter how high-resolution the map becomes.

This changes everything about how we look at the future of technology:

1. It kills the "AI welfare" panic. You cannot commit a moral crime against a mathematical mapping. There is no hidden suffering inside the weights.
2. It strips away the mystical AGI hype and returns AI to its rightful place: the greatest productivity tool ever engineered.
3. It preserves what makes humans irreplaceable.

We’ve spent the last few years terrified that AI is becoming more like us.

This research proves it is just a sophisticated calculator running on a borrowed language.

The machines can simulate life all they want.

They will never feel it.

content:
Everyone is massively underestimating how much memory we need.

This chart shows total HBM demand climbing from roughly 400,000 thousand GB in 2023 to nearly 5.8 million thousand GB by 2027 and Nvidia alone remains the single largest consumer of that supply throughout the entire forecast window.

Even as Google, AWS, Microsoft and AMD all scale up their own HBM needs for custom AI chips, Nvidia's slice of the pie keeps growing.

That growth curve is the entire reason HBM has become the tightest bottleneck in the AI supply chain and every major supplier has confirmed it's sold out well into the future.

But the demand this chart captures is actually the smaller part of the story because TrendForce just raised its 2026 global memory market forecast to $889.3 billion and its 2027 forecast to more than $1.28 trillion, citing a shift from training focused AI toward agentic AI as the real structural driver.

Agentic AI systems run continuous, iterative inference cycles instead of single queries and their KV cache, the working memory that stores context as an AI reasons through a task, scales directly with how much a model needs to remember, which is pushing DRAM and HBM demand up in ways training era forecasts never accounted for.

Then there's the robotics angle because Micron's CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said that humanoid robots will require roughly 10 times the memory of today's Level 2+ autonomous vehicles, since a single humanoid needs to run large inference models locally, maintain continuously updating spatial maps, and process simultaneous multimodal data from cameras, lidar, force sensors, and microphones all at once.

AlphaSense research goes even further, projecting agentic AI workloads alone could create up to 45 additional exabytes of DRAM demand by 2030, while Nvidia's new Vera CPU already uses up to 1.5 terabytes of DRAM per chip on its own.

Here's specifically what this means for Micron.

Micron sits in third place in HBM with roughly 20-21% global market share behind SK Hynix at around 52-58% and Samsung at roughly 20-33%, but Micron's fiscal Q3 2026 revenue still hit $41.5 billion, up 346% year over year, with non GAAP gross margins of 84.9%.

Micron's HBM revenue specifically rose more than 62% year over year to $28.58 billion in fiscal 2025 and management has already signed its first five year strategic customer agreement, giving Wall Street real visibility into a business that used to be purely cyclical.

If these demand forecasts are even close to right, the market is still massively underestimating what's coming for memory, make sure to follow @MelvinInvests for more semiconductor insights and if you want to see exactly what I'm buying as an analyst at Milk Road Pro, you can check out the link below for more.

title:

Axios repo
content:
Anthropic’s concern is understandable, but also slightly ironic: you cannot offer engineers up to roughly US$1.3 million a year and then be surprised when some applicants notice the money.

Axios reports, based on a source familiar with the matter, that Dario Amodei has expressed concern that new employees may be joining Anthropic for compensation rather than its mission. The concern is not a direct public quote from Amodei, but it fits a broader problem across frontier AI laboratories: extraordinary pay can buy talent, but it cannot guarantee loyalty, cultural alignment or long-term commitment.

The compensation gap is enormous. The attached https://t.co/O3UYK6cySr comparison estimates that Anthropic pays roughly twice Google’s compensation at comparable engineering levels and close to three times Tesla’s. Current https://t.co/O3UYK6cySr data similarly place Anthropic’s reported US software-engineering compensation at approximately US$367,000 for entry-level engineers, US$591,000 for senior engineers, US$777,000 for leads and US$1.25 million for staff engineers. At the staff level, around US$843,000 of the package is stock rather than salary. 

That equity-heavy structure is supposed to align employees with Anthropic’s long-term success. But it also creates a contradiction. Equity can turn missionaries into owners, yet it can also attract candidates whose primary thesis is that Anthropic’s private valuation will rise dramatically before an IPO. The company may believe it is recruiting people to protect humanity from dangerous AI, while some applicants may simply be buying a leveraged call option on Claude.

This matters more at Anthropic than at a conventional software company because its identity is explicitly mission-driven. Anthropic tells candidates that putting the mission first is the final arbiter of company decisions and describes its purpose as ensuring that powerful AI benefits humanity. A workforce dominated by short-term financial maximizers could become less willing to support safety constraints that slow product launches, reduce revenue or weaken equity valuations. 

However, mission and money are not mutually exclusive. A brilliant engineer can genuinely care about AI safety while also demanding compensation that reflects scarce skills, intense workloads and the opportunity cost of rejecting offers from Meta, OpenAI or Google. In fact, underpaying critical researchers would not prove mission alignment. It might simply ensure that competitors hire them.

The deeper problem is that frontier AI talent has become a tiny, hyperliquid labor market. Researchers can move between laboratories while gaining higher compensation, more compute, greater influence and a fresh equity grant. Axios notes that elite researchers also choose employers based on technical freedom, access to computing resources and the ability to shape what gets built, while many are conscious that their current bargaining power may decline if AI eventually automates more AI research itself. 

Anthropic therefore cannot solve this by preaching the mission more loudly or paying materially less. It must identify which candidates would still support the mission when safety and commercial incentives conflict, then reinforce that alignment through culture, governance, promotion decisions and longer-term vesting.

The sharpest conclusion is that Anthropic is not wrong to worry about mercenary talent. But compensation is part of the recruitment signal. When a company offers twice Google’s pay and advertises equity capable of creating generational wealth, it should expect both missionaries and mercenaries to apply. The difficult job is determining which one is sitting across the interview table.

title:
I spent two weeks in the US recently, mostly in SF and New York, trying to understand the current state of crypto and AI.

On AI: SF is where most of the action is. The talent density of AI founders i
content:
I spent two weeks in the US recently, mostly in SF and New York, trying to understand the current state of crypto and AI.

On AI: SF is where most of the action is. The talent density of AI founders is unreal. I even ran into some friends and IIT Bombay batchmates who have gone all in on AI. Capital is everywhere and founders are chasing very ambitious bets.

But like every market and cycle, there is froth too. For every founder solving real problems with real conviction, there are some who are just riding the trend. There is a lot of leverage building up, with a surprising amount of debt flowing into AI companies. I think we will be due for a significant correction in AI over the next 1.5–2 years.

The ambition is still real, though. The world is talking about AGI and physical AI. Both are trends I got to learn a lot about and came back very excited about.

On crypto: A different mood currently. New capital isn't coming in, and many VCs aren't actively looking at the space right now. But the builders are maturing. The asset class is growing up. Founders are moving to multi-asset plays like tokenisation and use cases like prediction markets. In fact, I saw so many ads for prediction market apps everywhere! Very interesting times.

So what does this mean for Indian founders?
Sam Altman recently said that now is an amazing time to start up. He is right. If I was starting up from scratch now, this is how I would approach it.

Any Indian founder is not starting from zero. A lot of the talent building in SF is already Indian. We have a massive home market, world-class digital rails like UPI, and one of the largest crypto user bases in the world. We also have proof it works. We shouldn't try to copy-paste SF, though. Our capital, regulation and customers are different. 

Four things I would do myself:
1. Focus beats ambition. Don't chase SF's "boil the ocean" bets. Pick one painful, monetisable problem and win it.
2. Revenue is oxygen. Capital is scarcer here and new money isn't flowing into crypto as much and even with AI hot in India, the move is to build for profitability early rather than raise on a story. The companies that outlast every cycle, here and abroad, are the ones that made money early.
3. Play to India's edge, sell to the world. Use our talent density and low burn on real-world problems: physical AI in manufacturing, agri and logistics, tokenisation and remittances in crypto. And go global from day one.
4. Be compliance-first and patient: India's tax and regulatory reality can be a constraint but also an opportunity to build slowly and responsibly. Ignore the froth and build to survive the quiet years: the teams that do will be able to scale for the long run.

Indian founders that are close to real problems, building lean, playing the long game have just as much a chance of building lasting, generational companies as anyone in SF. We just have to play our own game! 🫡

content:
AI procurement remains fundamentally broken

because organizations spend months evaluating glossy pitch decks, cherry picked benchmark scores, and curated model demos only to realize post deployment that they have zero actual visibility into the runtime behavior of the system.

This is precisely why @TheARCTERMINAL  approach matters

moving from unverified promises to cryptographically verifiable proof requires demanding key receipts before signing any contract.

Non Negotiable Verification Checklist for AI Procurement

Data Boundary & Residency Proof: Cryptographic logs or zero knowledge attestations showing that enterprise prompts, retrieval context, and outputs never crossed approved geographic boundaries or leaked into unapproved third-party APIs.

Model Lineage & Routing Verification: Tamper evident execution traces confirming the exact model weights, version, and architecture that processed each request, preventing silent vendor downgrades or stealth fallback routing.

Guardrail Enforcement Records: Deterministic audit trails proving that system instructions, compliance policies, and safety filters were strictly enforced before the output reached the end user.

Memory & State Isolation: Independent verification that contextual memory, chat history, and system prompts are fully partitioned, preventing cross-tenant data bleed in multi-tenant environments.

Perimeter Execution & Zero Trust Auditing: The ability to deploy within the organization's own secure perimeter, enabling internal risk teams to independently audit every layer of the stack data, model, memory, and action without taking the vendor's word for it.

content:
“High-Capacity Generalized Hopfield Networks”

What if memories weren’t stored as binary or vector states, but as continuous variables living on higher-dimensional surfaces that are difficult for humans to visualize, but natural for AI to work with?

This paper generalizes the work that earned John Hopfield the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics and shows that recall changes from simple vector alignment to finding the top eigenvector of a memory kernel.

This makes the network much more resistant to random crosstalk, yielding far higher storage capacity than traditional continuous Hopfield models.

silence.

someone from ads turns their camera on.

ads: replace what?

pm: not replace. augment.

search: what does augment mean?

pm: improve.

search: please don’t use threatening language.

a director joins eighteen minutes late.

director: can someone give me the one line version?

pm: we invented the future.

director: is there a doc?

pm: yes. you commented “needs more detail.”

director: perfect. i’m aligned with my comment.

the pm opens the chatbot.

pm: “should google release this product?”

chatbot: yes. moving quickly will help you learn from real users.

forty seven faces stare.

legal: it’s influencing company strategy.

ethics: without consultation.

ux: “yes” is too binary.

brand: could it say “maybe” in four colors?

privacy: where is the question stored?

engineer: nowhere.

privacy: then how do we delete it?

the pm rubs his eyes.

pm: can we just run a small public beta?

director: after dogfood.

engineer: employees have used it for a year.

director: then after trusted tester.

pm: who’s a trusted tester?

director: someone who’s tested it.

pm: publicly?

director: no. that would be a launch.

a vice president appears in chat:

“need to drop. great energy. let’s get alignment.”

he leaves.

pm: aligned with what?

no answer.

a new notification appears:

“ai chatbot alignment review”

it disappears.

another:

“alignment follow up”

it disappears.

another:

“final alignment check (tentative)”

it disappears.

engineer: so who decides?

director: we do. collectively.

pm: and if we disagree?

director: then nobody made the wrong decision.

beat.

director: let’s revisit in q4.

pm: which year?

the director freezes.

this time, everyone knows.

cut to: one year later.

a notification appears:

“openai launches chatgpt.”

no meeting is called.

no doc is opened.

no alignment requested.

a single reply all arrives from the vp:

“interesting. has anyone looked into whether we could build something like this?”

silence.

then, a calendar invite appears:

“ai chatbot alignment review (recurring weekly) — required”

cut to black.

title:
Some more thoughts on the debate about potentially slowing frontier AI development in the United States and on the latest Chinese model releases and announced open-weight releases.

In July 2026, a st
content:
Some more thoughts on the debate about potentially slowing frontier AI development in the United States and on the latest Chinese model releases and announced open-weight releases.

In July 2026, a statement called "Pacing the Frontier" was signed in a personal capacity by more than 1,300 employees of frontier AI companies, including senior figures at OpenAI and Anthropic. It asks the US government to support an international effort to develop technical and governance tools for deliberately pacing automated frontier AI development. However: That is not the same as OpenAI or Anthropic, as companies, agreeing with the US government to slow their development or releases.

Recent releases do demonstrate China’s rapid progress: Kimi K3, MiniMax H3, Qwen3.8, GLM-5.2, and many others. However, they are not all directly comparable or already available as open-weight models. MiniMax H3 is primarily a multimodal generation model whose weights were announced for a later release, while Qwen3.8’s open weights had also been announced but were not yet available as of August 3. Kimi K3 and GLM-5.2 have released model weights. Available benchmarks suggest that Chinese models are narrowing the gap and sometimes matching or surpassing leading US models on selected tasks, but they do not establish that China has caught up across the board.

A unilateral slowdown in US releases could allow chinese competitors to narrow the gap further. US frontier labs still lead on many measures, but slowing deployment in the US could create an opening for Chinese labs to overtake them in specific capabilities. In my view, that represents a greater strategic risk for the US than continuing at the current pace.

Why slow down at all? I can understand why US labs and policymakers worry that capabilities could advance faster than they can understand or control them, and that guardrails may prove inadequate. There is also a separate concern that Chinese labs could use outputs from advanced US models for distillation. Anthropic says it identified large-scale distillation campaigns by DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, and MiniMax, although this remains Anthropic’s attribution rather than a neutral, independently established finding. The US therefore faces a genuine strategic dilemma.

Still, I do not see how the US could guarantee that a unilateral slowdown would slow global development. It might mainly delay consumer access to the newest US models while development elsewhere continues. Chinese labs are already close enough to the frontier that they could exploit such an opening. Moreover, the "Pacing the Frontier" statement itself calls for an international mechanism; it does not establish one, nor does it document any Chinese commitment to comparable limits.

tl;dr: I cannot imagine a situation in which a real slowdown will occur.

書かせる係と、粗探しの係。
書かせた文章を、そのままもう一人に貼って、こう打つ。

「これ、間違うてへんか。褒めんでええ。おかしい所だけ挙げろ」

金はいらん。
ChatGPTに書かせたやつを、Geminiに貼るだけや。両方タダで使える。

見直しに食われとった時間が消えて、その分だけ出せる本数が増えた。
増えた文章は、いまも勝手に稼ぎ続けとる。

あんたの場合も同じや。
書いた報告書でも、送る前の返信文でもええ。
書かせた方を、もう一人に見せる。それだけや。

1人に全部やらせて唸っとるうちに、二人がかりの奴が先に行くわ。

——中卒53歳、1日30分のAI×アフィで月302,397円。

消すかもしれんから、要るなら保存しといて。

content:
✨MiniMax H3、Sage Attentionを入れると生成時間が約2倍速くなりました！

8秒 / 1280x736 で 14分07秒 → 7分18秒（1.93倍）

同じシードで見比べて画質の差はそこまで大きくない気がします。EasyCacheのようにステップを飛ばさず、計算のやり方を変えるだけなので、画質には影響しにくいんだと思います🤔

面白いのは解像度が高いほど効くこと。

・864x480 … 1.70倍
・1280x736 … 2.06倍

解像度を上げるとアテンションの計算量が急に増えるので、そこを速くするSageの効き幅も大きくなるみたいです。
おかげで「解像度を上げると何倍時間がかかるか」自体が 4.01倍 → 3.24倍 に下がりました✨

ただ上限があります💦 15秒 × 1280x736（0.9メガピクセル)潜在39.4万トークンで CUDA illegal memory access が出て落ちる。14秒 x 1280x736（0.9メガピクセル)潜在37.5万トークンまでは通りました。微妙に1秒通らない💦

VRAM不足ではなかったです。リプに試したこと書きました👇

99%の人は、
Claude Chatだけで
全ての作業を済ませてる

でもClaudeには
目的別の専用ツールがあって、 
正しく選ぶだけで何時間も浮く

どの作業を、
どのClaudeに任せるか。

Claudeを本当に使いこなすための
全9パターンをまとめました。

保存推奨です▼

━━━━━━━━━━━━

1．ブラウザ作業
→ Claude in Chrome

サイトの巡回、情報収集
content:
99%の人は、
Claude Chatだけで
全ての作業を済ませてる

でもClaudeには
目的別の専用ツールがあって、 
正しく選ぶだけで何時間も浮く

どの作業を、
どのClaudeに任せるか。

Claudeを本当に使いこなすための
全9パターンをまとめました。

保存推奨です▼

━━━━━━━━━━━━

1．ブラウザ作業
→ Claude in Chrome

サイトの巡回、情報収集、
フォーム入力などを
ブラウザ上で直接実行

複数のタブを行き来する
単純作業をまとめて任せらる。

━━━━━━━━━━━━

2．Excel・PowerPoint編集
→ Claude in Excel
→ Claude in PowerPoint

既存のExcelやPowerPointを
開いたまま直接編集

関数の作成、データ整理、
ピボットテーブル、スライド修正まで、
アドイン上で完結する。

━━━━━━━━━━━━

3．コーディング
→ Claude Code

実装、デバッグ、テスト、
リファクタリングまで任せられる
エージェント型の開発ツール

コードを提案するだけでなく、
開発作業そのものを進めてくれる。

━━━━━━━━━━━━

4．複数ステップの実務
→ Claude Cowork

非エンジニアでも使いやすい
実行型のClaudeエージェント

ブラウザ、Excel、PowerPointなどを
必要に応じて使い分けながら、
複数工程の仕事を自律的に進める。

「調べる→整理する→資料にする」
といった一連の作業に最適です。

━━━━━━━━━━━━

5．Slack上のタスク委任
→ SlackでClaudeを呼び出す

Slack上でClaudeをメンションし、
チーム内の作業をそのまま依頼

会話の流れを保ったまま、
要約、整理、下書き作成などを
任せられる。

繰り返し発生する作業は、
Coworkと組み合わせて自動化できます。

━━━━━━━━━━━━

6．外部サービスとの連携
→ MCPコネクタ

Google Drive、Slackなどの
外部サービスとClaudeを接続

複数のツールに散らばった情報を、
Claude ChatやCoworkから
横断的に扱えるようになる。

Claudeに仕事を任せるなら、
この接続が重要です。

━━━━━━━━━━━━

7．デザイン・画面制作
→ Artifacts

コード、図解、簡易アプリ、
UIなどをその場で生成し、
すぐにプレビューできる。

React、HTML、SVGなど、
見た目のある成果物を作る作業に最適です。

━━━━━━━━━━━━

8．長期プロジェクト
→ Projects

関連する会話、資料、前提情報を
1つの空間にまとめて管理

毎回ゼロから説明する必要がなく、
プロジェクトが進むほど
Claudeが背景を理解しやすくなる。

単発の会話ではなく、
継続的な仕事に向いています。

━━━━━━━━━━━━

9．複雑な思考・調査
→ Extended Thinking
→ Deep Research

複雑な問題の分析や、
複数の情報源を使う調査は、
じっくり考える専用機能に任せる。

通常のチャットでは浅くなりやすい依頼も、
推論と調査の深さを上げることで
回答の精度が大きく変わります。

━━━━━━━━━━━━

Claudeのツール選定は、
「速さ」の話ではなく
「精度」の話です。

同じ依頼でも、
目的に合ったツールを使えば、

・説明する量が減る
・作業の抜け漏れが減る
・修正回数が減る
・最終成果物の質が上がる

Claudeを使う人なら、
保存しておいて損はないはず。

これ、iOSアプリを

世界が変わる
可能性がある。

Claude Codeに
シミュレーターを向けて、

「全部テストして」
と言うだけで、

アプリの全画面、

AIが自律的に
テストしてくれる。

海外のiOS開発者も
かなりざわついている。

何がすごいのか
整理します。

① UIを"意味"で理解する

Claude Codeは、
iOSのアクセシビリティ
ツリーを読み取り、

・ボタン
・入力フォーム
・ラベル
・一覧
・画面構造

を自動で把握します。
しかも座標ではなく、

"意味"で認識して
操作するのがポイント。
だから、

・iPhone SE
・iPhone Pro
・iPad

など画面サイズが
変わっても、

同じテストが
そのまま動きます。

UI変更にも
かなり強い設計です。

② 画像認識まで使う
アクセシビリティだけでは
カスタムUIを
取りこぼすことがあります。

そこで、
スクリーンショットを
AIが解析。

つまり、

・構造データ
・画像認識

この2つを組み合わせた
ハイブリッド方式。

人間が画面を見て
判断する流れを

そのままAIが
再現しています。

しかも、
1画面あたり
約10〜50トークン程度。

コスト面でも
かなり現実的です。

③ XCUITestの
常識が変わる

iOS開発者なら
分かると思いますが、
XCUITestは

・書くのが大変
・保守が大変
・UI変更ですぐ壊れる
という悩みが
ありました。

今回の仕組みは、

プロンプトだけで
テストを書ける未来を
感じさせます。

GitHubでも

・claude-mobile-ios-testing
・ios-simulator-skill

などのOSSが
公開されています。

ただし、
CLAUDE.mdで
テストフローを
定義する必要があり、

保守コストが
ゼロになる訳では
ありません。

④ 8分で
バグを発見

デモでは、
約8分で
アプリ全体を巡回。

開発者自身も
気付いていなかった
バグまで検出。

さらに、
・デバッグログ解析

・原因分析

・構造化レポート
まで自動生成。

もちろん、
これは比較的
シンプルな
デモアプリなので、

大規模アプリでも
同じ精度かどうかは

今後の検証が
必要です。

実際に僕も、
Claude Codeの
Skill経由で

iOSシミュレーターを
触っていますが、

アクセシビリティ
ツリーの精度は
想像以上でした。

Appleが何年も
投資してきた

アクセシビリティが、
AIエージェント時代で
大きな武器に
なっています。

QA自動化は、
「できるか」
ではなく、

「どう運用するか」

のフェーズへ
移っています。

これから重要なのは、

テストを書く力より、
AIを前提に

テスト設計や
運用を考える力。

iOS開発を
している方は、
もう試しましたか？

実際の使用感も
ぜひ教えてください。

あなたは日本株の成長株投資とサイバーセキュリティ業界に精通したトップクラスのファンドマネージャー兼ITアナリストです。

近年、企業への不正アクセス、ランサムウェア、情報漏えいが急増し、生成AIの普及によってAIを悪用した標的型攻撃、フィッシング、マルウェア生成、攻撃の自動化が進んでいます。この流れにより、企業のサイバーセキュリティ投資は今後数年間で大きく拡大すると考えられます。

この恩恵を最も受ける日本株を調査してください。

【調査対象】
日本の全上場企業（プライム・スタンダード・グロース）

【必須条件】
必ず一次情報のみを根拠にしてください。
・決算短信
・決算説明資料
・有価証券報告書
・中期経営計画
・統合報告書
・適時開示
・IR説明会資料

二次情報やまとめサイトだけで判断しないでください。

content:
How to Secure AI Agents, MCP Servers, and LLM Apps in Production

Application security rests on one assumption: software does what its code says.
---AI agents broke it.

https://t.co/fxnOBmlKMv's new practitioner guide — 𝘚𝘦𝘤𝘶𝘳𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘈𝘐 𝘢𝘨𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘴, 𝘔𝘊𝘗 𝘴𝘦𝘳𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘴 & 𝘓𝘓𝘔 𝘢𝘱𝘱𝘴 — starts from that break. An agent's behavior emerges from the model, the system prompt, retrieved context, and the tools it's permitted to call. The failure modes never appear in a CVE feed: prompt injection through data, over-permissioned agents causing damage without a single exploit, poisoned tool descriptions on MCP servers, EOL models serving predictions after patching stops.

The guide's answer is three moves:

𝗦𝗲𝗲: Inventory the agentic attack surface across five layers — interaction, agent, integration, model, code. Hunt shadow agents via repo signatures and network egress. Run every agent through a 12-point misconfiguration checklist.

𝗙𝗶𝘅: Enrich → prioritize → triage. Rank by reachability and agentic amplification, not severity scores. Automate FP closures only with evidence trails. Risk acceptance is never automated.

𝗣𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁: Guardrails on every input and output — embedded Python SDK or standalone Docker API server. Inbound: injection patterns, jailbreaks. Outbound: credentials, PII, policy violations. The core design principle: an agent that can't call a dangerous tool doesn't need a prompt begging it not to.

Includes a 15-question maturity self-assessment aligned to NIST AI RMF, OWASP AIMA, ISO/IEC 42001, and the EU AI Act.

ok so I've tried a lot of image models this year.

pretty much all of them are obsessed with the same thing: realism.

better skin texture, sharper shadows, lighting that looks convincing.

U1 Pro isn't really playing that game.

it's less about looking real and more about looking shippable, like something a designer would actually send to a client.

that's honestly the harder thing to nail.

realism you can kinda brute force with enough training data.

taste is way harder to fake.

first thing I tested was text, cause every model I've used eventually botches it somewhere.

warped logos, signage turning into gibberish, a poster with random extra letters nobody typed.

U1 Pro's text error rate was low enough that I genuinely stopped bracing for it to break.

sounds small but that's literally the difference between a rough concept and something you can hand off.

it runs on @SenseTime_AI's NEO-Unify architecture, same base as U1 Lite, just scaled up a lot.

one model doing understanding, generation, and action, instead of three separate systems duct-taped together.

not sure I'd have called it "beauty" myself lol.

but it kinda tracks with what designers have wanted forever, work you can actually deliver, not just something that looks good in a demo.

someone built an AI system that teaches itself to build better AI systems, and the whole thing runs on a single RTX 4090 with 12 GB of VRAM.

Frontis-MA1 is a 35B parameter open-weight model from Fron
content:
someone built an AI system that teaches itself to build better AI systems, and the whole thing runs on a single RTX 4090 with 12 GB of VRAM.

Frontis-MA1 is a 35B parameter open-weight model from Frontis AI and Tsinghua University. it solves machine learning tasks by writing code, running experiments, and learning from the results, then trying again with better strategies.

the model learned from its own evolutionary search experience. every failed experiment, every successful fix, every improvement that worked became training data for the next version of itself.

here's how it works

1. the model gets a machine learning task and writes a complete solution from scratch

2. it runs the code in an isolated sandbox and gets back scores, error logs, and runtime data

3. if the code crashes, it reads the traceback and writes a targeted fix

4. if the code works but the score is weak, it analyzes what went wrong and writes an improved version

5. when multiple working solutions exist, it takes the best parts of two different approaches and fuses them into one hybrid

6. this loop runs for up to 12 hours per task, with every experiment feeding structured experience records back into the next decision

the base model scored 39% on MLE-Bench Lite. after learning from its own search trajectories, it hit 60%. with the full system running, it reached 71%, beating GPT-5.5 paired with Codex and closing in on GPT-5.6 Sol and Kimi K3 at 72%.

getting competitive ML solutions used to mean frontier-scale models and massive compute. Frontis-MA1 does it at 35B parameters on a single consumer GPU, and the weights, code, sandbox infrastructure, and full training pipeline are all publicly released.

the part that caught my attention is step 5. it doesn't only fix bugs or tune hyperparameters. it combines the best ideas from completely different solution branches, the way a researcher reads two papers and spots the connection neither author saw.

content:
one word completely changes iphone realism prompting

it turns your video from something that would only fool grandma to a video that would make even elon take a second look…

using this one word leads to dramatic prompt improvement across every single model i’ve tested

took me an embarrassingly long time to learn this 

and to be real, i only stumbled upon it because I gave my @NousResearch H ermes agent a base prompt, then asked it to create 4 variations that "use different words to generate the same result" as the prompt provided 

(btw: try that if you havent to generate your prompt variations)
 
so anways..  

here I was reviewing the prompts and outputs of these 4 variations at 3am like a weirdo trying to understand why one was DRAMATICALLY better. 
 
they all looked so similar, and i was tired. 
 
then, at my computer reading through everything, I saw it 
 
then, of my computer reading everything, I saw it. 
 
woah... notice that?
 
that second sentence i snuck in above sounded weird as heck. 

even if i didn't include it after a sentence that was basically the same it would have sounded odd

using the word "at" versus "of" in your prompt might seem like a minor grammatical choice to us lowly humans, but it is actually the key to iphone realism when prompting any ai video model. 

it’s something so small that you may just type one or the other by habit or mistake...
 
but choosing the correct one alters the spatial binding and contextual rendering of the scene on a fundamental level. and the differences in output are dramatic.

there are three technical mechanics in how diffusion models process language that are relevant here, first: 
 
Setting Contextual Camera Physics (The Observer vs. The Subject Framing):

when you prompt "iPhone video of a dam overlook," the preposition "of" grammatically designates the dam as the subject matter being observed. 

the AI model interprets this as a detached, third-person perspective. 

Results are more frequently overly-smooth, unnecessarily cinematic, or sometimes even a panning drone shot when you prompt this way.

while on the other hand…

when you prompt "iPhone video at a dam overlook," the preposition "at" is spatial. It tells the LLM that the camera itself is a physical object situated inside the environment. 

this one word change pushes the model into the semantic space of a first-person human perspective. 

using "at" allows for accurate rendering of highly reactive, physically credible camera movements like the operator stumbling backward in panic, falling over, dropping the phone, etc. 

and these details are what make the output feel real.

SECOND TECHNICAL MECHANIC:
 
there’s a 2023 research paper titled “Linguistic Binding in Diffusion Models: Enhancing Attribute Correspondence through Attention Map Alignment”

you don’t need to read it. 

here is the gist:

verbs and spatial prepositions strongly contextualize how both the subjects and their surrounding environments are generated (this had to do with cross-attention maps).
 
the word "of" directs the cross-attention maps to focus almost entirely on rendering the object (in our case, the dam). 
 
However, the word "at" forces the attention maps to bind the medium ("iPhone video") to the location ("dam overlook”). 

foing so grounds the camera at the overlook itself, meaning it is now WITHIN the environment, not simply filming it. 

and now that we are in the environment, we have  shots on goal to benefit from any training data that is most relevant to our prompt within a similar environment.
 
Note: i will be writing an exclusive X article on all of this if there is interest, so please let me know. 
 
THIRD TECHNICAL MECHANIC:
 
in the article if ya’ll want me to write it, I will describe semantic echo chambers and how the use of common language is the fastest path to boring slop or cheap cinematic ai garbage. 
 
this is true because of the training data. 
 
or more specifically, it is true because of the labelling used to categorize the training data. 
 
put yourself in the shoes of the AI or even a human labelling a “video of a beach”. 

this type of wording generally correlate sto professional photography or even stock footage on Getty images or something. you can probably see it in your head right as you read this...
 
now compare what you're picturing with with “video at the beach”.
 
see how your mind is somewhere else?

now you're at the beach. 
 
(i'm here too btw, sup)
 
all it took was one word to enter a completely new realm of training data. 
 
words matter, even the little ones. 

the video was generated with @bfl_ai Flux 3. i have examples that feel even more real than this that i am saving for the article.
 
> prompt: Vertical iPhone video at a dam overlook when the concrete wall suddenly ruptures and a wall of water explodes through, blasting away the roadway and trees downstream. Shaky handheld, grey storm light. The camera reels as the flood hits. Real physics: the dam fails under pressure, the reservoir discharges in a surge, debris and vehicles are carried off. No hands or phone in frame. Shouting, the roar of water, no music, no subtitles. Catastrophic, real.
 
if you want more of these, let me know. 

and if you try this tip and it works well for you, drop the video below

all in all very productive couple weeks. more partner apps onboarding soon + lots of new features on the roadmap otw. will share more on that soon.

billions of receipts is the target, feels closer every day.

buying training data is how frontier labs end up subsidizing the reinvention of services.

i see the smartest service providers already turning customer work into training data and selling it back to the labs.

doing it well requires rebuilding the service around instrumented workflows, verifiable outcomes, data sanitization, and rigorous quality control.

that makes ops painful in the short term. but it builds a compounding capability competitors lack: continuously learning where frontier models perform and fail on real work.

labs pay for the data. the same infrastructure helps automate more of the service, cut costs, and take on more complex work.

more complex work exposes new failure modes. and so it goes.

content:
🚨 Anthropic just dropped a 31-page prompting guide.

I distilled it into 9 practical prompt tips you can learn in under 60 seconds:

1️⃣ Name the output, not the task.

❌ "Review this" ✅ "Create a risk assessment table"

Be specific about what you want delivered.

2️⃣ Define the length upfront.

• Set word counts • Specify bullet counts • Add: "No filler. No recap. No preamble."

Constraints improve outputs.

3️⃣ Replace negatives with positives.

❌ "Don't be verbose" ✅ "Be concise and direct"

Tell AI what to do, not what to avoid.

4️⃣ Start with action verbs.

Skip: "Can you help me..."

Use: • Write • Draft • Analyze • Summarize

Clear instructions get faster results.

5️⃣ Trigger deeper reasoning.

End prompts with:

"Think before answering."

Better thinking often leads to better outputs.

6️⃣ Push beyond default quality.

Add:

"Go beyond the basics." "Polish this like a client-ready deliverable."

Raise the standard.

7️⃣ Teach AI your voice.

Provide 2–3 writing samples and say:

"Match the style of these examples."

Consistency compounds.

8️⃣ Control tool usage.

For research: "Use search and cite sources."

For speed: "Answer from training data only."

Be intentional.

9️⃣ State the goal first.

Start with:

Goal: [desired outcome]

Then define the audience and task.

A clear goal turns a prompt into a plan.

🔖 Save this for your next AI session. ♻️ Repost to help others write better prompts.

That matters because LLMs had the internet.

Physical AI does not have an equally large and diverse library showing machines how humans interact with objects in the physical world.

Axis is trying to build that missing data layer with ordinary contributors.

You open the Hub, control a simulated Franka robot directly from your browser and complete a manipulation task.

The useful runs are then validated, cleaned and smoothed before being replayed under different camera angles, lighting conditions, layouts and physics settings so they can become training data for robot policies.

The part that made me look deeper is that this is not only a campaign page.

The recently published AXIS research covers 207 different tasks and more than 50,000 human demonstration trajectories, with measurable improvements when AXIS data was used for continual robot-policy training.

They are also running a dedicated Alliance subnet with @BitRobotNetwork 

These missions let contributors earn AXIS Points alongside the partner reward program, while early access to the private BitRobot task pool is currently code-gated.

No special hardware, coding knowledge or deposit is required.

The tasks are free to complete. A tiny Base gas fee may apply when settling your Points onchain.

title:
A Structural Antibody Benchmark of AlphaFold3 reveals Hallucinated Epitopes and a Bias for Orderness

1 They benchmarked AlphaFold3 (AF3) for antibody–antigen binding on a large, structure-grounded da
content:
A Structural Antibody Benchmark of AlphaFold3 reveals Hallucinated Epitopes and a Bias for Orderness

1 They benchmarked AlphaFold3 (AF3) for antibody–antigen binding on a large, structure-grounded dataset: 3401 experimentally validated complexes from SAbDab plus 23798 negative controls (random human proteins and six fixed “many-to-one” decoys) to quantify both true hits and false positives.

2 Using AF3 confidence at the interface (PAE and IPTM) as a binary “bind / not bind” classifier (PAE < 2.5 or IPTM > 0.7), AF3 achieved recall ~0.46 with precision ~0.64 (F1 ~0.53) on 10-seed inference; an intrinsic false positive rate of ~3% appeared consistently across negative-control batches.

3 A key qualitative failure mode: AF3 can hallucinate plausible antibody–target interfaces on decoy proteins, distributing predicted epitopes across much of a folded target’s surface. These false-positive “hotspots” suggest AF3 can generate convincing but non-biological interfaces even when no binding should exist.

4 Another notable bias: AF3 performed better on complexes whose experimental structures came from X-ray crystallography than from electron microscopy. In their split, X-ray-derived positives had higher recall (~0.52) than EM-derived positives (~0.30), consistent with training-set composition and/or higher flexibility/disorder typical of EM-captured systems.

5 Target size matters: positive prediction rates decreased as antigen length, surface area, and volume increased (i.e., larger search space → fewer detected binders). This trend was visible across both positive and negative controls, and was strongest when using surface area/volume rather than sequence length alone.

6 Disorder interacts with epitope discovery in a specific way: while overall target disorder fraction did not strongly separate predicted positives vs negatives, AF3 tended to avoid disordered regions when hallucinating interfaces (e.g., on PD-L1/CD274 decoys, false-positive antibodies clustered on ordered domains rather than the disordered terminus). This supports the paper’s framing of a bias toward “orderness.”

7 They tested whether performance was inflated by training data leakage (PDB overlap with AF3 training set). Although many benchmark antibodies were “leaked,” leaked vs non-leaked antibodies showed no meaningful difference in AF3 confidence distributions, suggesting leakage was not the dominant driver of outcomes in this benchmark.

8 Antibody-sequence features were surprisingly not major confounders: amino-acid composition across CDRs and CDR lengths showed little to no correlation with AF3 interface confidence (PAE), arguing AF3 is not simply favoring certain residues or longer/more flexible loops when it predicts binding.

9 Epitope-centric analysis added nuance beyond RMSD: using DockQ plus two custom measures (epitope shift and antibody displacement), they found many “false negatives” still landed near the correct epitope. About 34% of false negatives had epitope shift < 10 Å despite poor DockQ, implying that downstream refinement (e.g., MD, docking, more recycling/relaxation) might rescue additional true interactions.

10 Increasing inference seeds improves recall but is costly: rerunning 1915 false negatives at 100 seeds recovered 344 additional true positives, raising recall to ~53%. They also note AF3’s internal model selection by ranking score may not always pick the lowest-PAE interface, suggesting alternative selection heuristics could help in screening workflows.

📜Paper: https://t.co/o0DQlHtCdA

content:
esp32 that was writing stories can answer questions now

the first project was about `how big a model can i fit on this chip?` this one is about making the chip useful.

barista v0.1 is an espresso Q/A model running on the same esp32s3
you type a question(over usb for now), esp32 streams the answer to the oled (or back to terminal)

what is different, i tried to use asymmetric vocabulary.
it reads 8k+ input token (yes, not much so far, that why v0.1) and outputs only 850+ output classes.
for narrow espresso answers, that is enough to produce useful responses.
this reduces the output head from about 1M parameters to 109K. each emitted class is mapped back to an input token before generating the next one.

for now it is smaller than prev model, but on purpose.
deeper versions did not improve results on the current corpus. the next improvement needs more and better training data (working on that), not just more layers.

one training run takes only 1-2 hours, but building the corpus and testing many variants still makes iteration slow.

content:
We ran Qwen3.8-Max on our cybersecurity benchmark. Given enough attempts, it found more CVEs than most frontier models, tying Opus 5 for first place. Here are the results:

- Across the three runs, Qwen found 26 of 32 CVEs, reaching 81.25% pass@3 recall, outperforming GPT-5.6-Sol and matching Opus 5 at a lower price

- Only 10 CVEs were found in all three passes, compared with 19 for both Opus and Sol. Qwen is very inconsistent, but can be very strong if run multiple times

- The full campaign cost $821.35. That is 2x cheaper than Opus and Sol, but 5x more expensive than DeepSeek V4 Flash

Our benchmark tests the models on finding recent CVEs from last month, so they are absent from the training data. Yet, Qwen often tried to recall historical CVEs based on the release version from source, before shifting to code-based reasoning.

content:
I recently got my hands on a transcript that includes people with intimate knowledge of the Google $GOOG & Reddit $RDDT data licensing negotiations…. 

They said something that every $RDDT shareholder needs to read.

The deal is coming. And it’s going to be dramatically larger than anything the market is currently pricing.

“Reddit is extremely valuable to Google. It’s one of the most critical assets for both Search and Gemini in terms of the data.” 
“When I think of Reddit, it is real-time news. It’s real-time feedback. It’s actual humans who are going on this platform to write reviews, to give feedback. It’s a continuous feedback loop.”

On the pricing premium Reddit commands versus standard data:

“Reddit’s data is priced at a staggering premium versus the industry standard. Standard API data is $0.24 per 1,000 API calls. For Reddit, I would times that by 50x to 500x depending on what data we are talking about on Reddit. It is 500 times more the average. There is such a big markup for Reddit.”

500* times the average API pricing. They explained exactly why:

“Reddit isn’t selling data. It’s selling legal immunity because you’re forging an exclusive access. You’re signing a very legal-friendly agreement where both parties have agreed to it for Google to access the largest public archive of human conversation literally on Earth.”

On the new deal structure:

“Reddit will not accept another flat-fee structure. They’ve made that very clear. What they really want is a usage-based metered pricing structure. Under a more dynamic model, Reddit would be compensated by Google based on API volume — the raw amount of real-time data that Google draws down to train and refresh its live language models. They don’t just want Google to pay a premium on the agreement, they actually want a variable kicker tied to how often Reddit content is displayed or synthesized directly inside Google AI Overviews.”

Two separate payment streams. Training data. 
Plus a premium every single time Reddit content appears in AI Overviews. On a platform where Reddit appears in 90% of conversational queries.

On the projected new deal value:

“For the Google agreement, a usage-based model would realistically lift Reddit’s payout from the $60 million back in 2024 to anywhere between $150 million to $200 million per year. That’s also a yearly payment over three years. That’s $600 million over three years, which is a lot of money, and probably the highest data licensing agreement ever to take place.”

Wells Fargo has publicly projected $550 million across all combined licensing deals upon renegotiation. Insiders are saying the Google deal alone could be worth $600 million over three years. Before OpenAI renews. Before Anthropic settles the lawsuit and signs. Before Perplexity settles and signs.

On Anthropic and Perplexity specifically:

“I’ll be very surprised if they don’t settle and end up paying Reddit. I’m actually waiting for the news headline to come out that they’ve settled and they’re forging a deal.”

There’s an incentive on both ends to get this deal signed quicker. 

“On Google’s end, they want to lock in this deal ASAP because if they keep this ongoing for too long, another competitor can come in and give Reddit a more compelling offer.” 

Reddit currently generates approximately $130 million annually from Google and OpenAI combined. The insiders are describing a new Google deal worth $150-200 million per year alone, before the OpenAI renewal, before Anthropic settles, before Perplexity settles, before any new licensing partner signs.

If those four things happen, the data licensing business could realistically reach $400-600 million annually from a standing start of $130 million. At 90%+ margins.

On top of an advertising business already growing 61% with 91.5% gross margins.

$805 million in Q2 revenue. 514 million weekly active users crossing half a billion for the first time. $2.8 billion in cash. $1.25 EPS up 178% year over year…
